full_judgment:
4. In the trial, the prosecution examined as many 'as 8 (eight) out of 18 (eighteen) witnesses, cited in the charge sheet, submitted by the investigating officer. After closure of the prosecution witnesses, the appellant present in the dock, was examined under section 342 of the, Code of Criminal Procedure who reiterated his innocence but he did not adduce any evidence in support of his; defence story. The defence case as it transpires from the trend of cross-examination that no occurrence took place on 'the date, time and place in the" manner as alleged and, the appellant had been falsely implicated in the case out of enmity and further pleaded that father of the appellant had a property around the house of the, informant who sought some land from him but when he refused to give the same to her, then she made the complaint on a false story. The trial court, considering the evidence on record as well as facts and circumstances of the case, found the appellant guilty, of the offence and convicted him with a sentence as mentioned above. The appellant; being aggrieved by and,' dissatisfied with the impugned' judgment and order of conviction and sentence; has presented this, appeal. 

 5. Mr Abdur Razzak, the learn Advocate, taking permission from this court on behalf of the learned Advocate Mr SM Rezaul Karim, submits, that the informant as alleged in the FIR that at the time 'of occurrence the accused by showing a knife in fear of life threatening aped her, whereas that knife was absent in the, proceeding of the case. He submits that there is no medical examination report as to the rape of the' victim, therefore, the prosecution failed to prove the concrete allegation of rape. In support, of this contention, he, has referred to the case of Zitu Ahsan alias Apon vs State, reported in.59 DLR 528. He further submits that there are so many contradictions available in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. Sustaining conviction on an allegation like rape, the evidence of witnesses has to corroborate each other but in the present case it is purely absent. In this contention, he has cited a case of Seraj Talukder vs State, reported in 3 BLC 182. He contends that there is no independent, disinterested and impartial witness who supported the allegation of rape, adding that if there is no evidence of independent witness, conviction cannot be sustained. He has relied upon a case of Hossain Shially (Fakir) vs State, reported in 56 DLR 637. He lastly submits that the charge is defective, not curable in law as the appellant was not examined properly under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, as such, the whole trial is liable to be vitiated and the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence is liable to be set-aside. 

 6. Mr AKM Zahirul Huq, the learned Deputy Attorney-General along with Mr. Md Asaduzzaman appearing on behalf of the Respondent-State, submit that the prosecution could be able to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt by examining the good and impartial witnesses. He further submits that the PW 1 as informant lodged the complaint before the police and she made statement before a competent magistrate, both of which versions are similar to each other and the evidence of PW 1 supported the FIR as well as statement, given by the victim under section 21 of the Ain, therefore, the trial court rightly and correctly passed the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence against the appellant. 

 7. Now let us see the evidence as to whether the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence passed by the trial court against the appellant were justified or not. 

 14. Heard the learned Advocates of both the parties, perused the evidence and materials on record and impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence, wherefrom it transpires that the prosecution brought the allegation of rape against the appellant contending that the appellant on the day of occurrence around 10-00 pm at night entered the hut of the victim by breaking fence and forcibly committed rape on her. 

 15. On a careful scrutiny of the evidence on record, we do not find any evidence of sign of violence as to the rape of the victim. It is very curious to us that the doctor who examined the person of the victim as alleged, was not produced by the prosecution before the trial court for examination of his report. It is also curious to us that there is no medical report of the victim, who was examined by Doctor, with the Lower Courts record and the prosecution failed to mark the same as exhibit. In this respect, we may cite a case of Biplob vs State, reported in 6 BLC 633 wherein it was held that:- 

 17. On perusal of their evidence on record, it appears that they all were connected' with the relationship of the victim as well as the informant. So we do not find any independent or neutral witness who gave evidence against the convict-appellant. Therefore, the prosecution case became doubtful, Here we may refer to the case of Hossain Shially (Fakirt vsState, reported in 56 DLR 637, it was observed that: 

 "The evidence of a prosecutrix in a rape case customarily, being a woman of full age, is not accepted as sufficient, but requires corroboration by independent evidence in order to be believed which hasbeen found in the decision reported in 19 DLR (SC) 259. 

 Added with this, in a case of allegation of rape where there is no independent eye- witness and the only evidence that of the prosecutrix herself and of those of whom it was reported, the Courts are not left with any objective test of gauging the truth of the story of the prosecutrix. Expert examination of the person of the prosecutrix or the garments had worn at the time and of the place where the rape took place is sine-qua-non in such cases. But in the instant case, the prosecution failed to 'satisfy all these points, inasmuch as evidence on record in no way justify the prosecution case. In few of such facts and 'circumstances, we 'find' no other alternative but to hold that the prosecution has withheld some important witnesses for the reason best known to them and on the other hand, has come with some neighbors whose evidence is in no; Way satisfactory as independent 'persons about their bonafide in the matter." 

 18. It is further noted here that the sketch map with 'index was marked as exhibit 3/1, wherefrom it appears that where the occurrence took place, the victim stayed' in the barinda of the house i.e, in the "C" marked place of the sketch map, leaving the main room of the house but why?, it has not been answered by prosecution evidence. It further appears from the form under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that some gaps were not filled up by, the concerned trial court at the time of examination of the accused and it is now simply seen blank, therefore, the examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is' seemed to be defective. However, we find that there are so many contradictions; available in the evidence of witnesses, particularly, in between the, statement of victim and the evidence: as presented by her in court. Moreso, absence of sign of rape and non- examination of the wearing clothes of the victim, also make the prosecution case shaky. In this contention, we may cite a case of Seraj Talukder vs State, reported in 3 BLC 182 wherein their Lordships opined that: 

 "There   are many contradictions in the evidence of the PWs and in between the statement made in ejahar and in the evidence as adduced in Court, and that absence of sign of rape in the medical report and non examination of the wearing clothes made the whole case most ,doubtful one and the prosecution has totally failed to prove their case beyond all reasonable' doubt and the appellant is not found guilty of the charge brought against him under section 6(1) of the ,Niui-o-Shishu Nirjatan (Bishes Bidhan) Ain, 1995." 

 19. It reveals from the evidence on record that the informant dig not file the case directly with the concerned police station rather placed the same before the superintendent of police of Pirojpur District and why did she go directly to the superintendent of police ignoring the local police station, it had not been satisfactorily explained neither in the ejahar nor in the given evidence of any witnesses. From the aforesaid discussion it appears to us that the prosecution has miserably failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. 

 20. In this regard, a decision may be relied upon a case of Mazharul alias Bhulan vs State, reported in 10 BLC 209 where their Lordships opined that, "After careful, examination and scrutiny of the evidence on record it appears that the prosecution could not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the victim was raped in the "pan baraj" and the appellant committed rape on her in the manner, place and time as alleged. Hence the benefit of such doubt will go in favour of the appellant, who is entitled to be acquitted."
